chapter: Later years and the Texas scene
title: Returning to the horn: Bill Russell and Southland
summary: Interviews by Bill Russell and Joe Mares persuaded Albert to play his horn again after he'd stopped.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Did you, when you came back from time to time, did you have any fans ever in the 40s for, you know, just to say a one night job? Or would you appear as a guest any time?

The only time I became interested in playing my horn again is when Joe Moray is asking me to come and make the Southland record. I had stopped playing all together and just laid the horn down. But when this came about, and no, I'll have to go back a little further. What's his name over at the Preservation Hall that takes the interview? It was my good friend. Bill Rosso. He plays the violin.

Yeah, Bill came to San Antonio and he interviewed me. And he asked me, why don't you play your horn again? And I said, well, I don't see anywhere where I can play what I know how to play. He said, man, it's going to come back. So finally, I said, well, okay, I'll take a shot. I kind of got my horn out and I started to practice. And then Joe Moray, like I said, was responsible for me being as active now as I am, plus a low influence from, what's his name? We just mentioned. Bill Russell. Bill Russell. Okay.
